history.title: Auth
gaps: Retest of g62-1 ('why mobile favors tokens'), via a fresh WebView scenario rather than the original question: initial answer was uncertain rather than firmly wrong (correctly guessed it depends on whether WebView has a cookie store, but couldn't confirm). Explained that a WebView is an embedded browser engine (Chromium/WebKit) carrying the full HTTP stack including the cookie jar, vs. a plain native app which has no browser engine and makes raw calls with no built-in cookie handling. Confirmed understood on follow-up. Worth a light confirm-only check next review rather than a full re-teach.

Fresh gap, surfaced on an HttpOnly/XSS scenario: conflated a missing SameSite flag with enabling the XSS attacker to steal-and-replay the cookie from their own machine. Corrected by separating CSRF (a blind forged request the victim's own browser fires and attaches the cookie to -- the attacker never sees the value) from theft-and-replay (governed entirely by HttpOnly, independent of SameSite). Craig pushed back with the legitimate observation that missing SameSite does enable CSRF, and from there correctly re-derived that theft-and-replay specifically was not possible in this scenario given HttpOnly was set. Worth a light confirm-only check next review.

history.title: Auth
gaps: Fresh scenario (lookalike phishing domain) tested with the cookie value framing; conflated domain scoping with SameSite/CSRF on first pass — corrected after clarification that a cookie is never sent to a domain other than the one that set it, independent of any flag. Confirmed understood on follow-up: distinguished domain scoping (wrong-domain case), SameSite (forged request to right domain from elsewhere), and HttpOnly (partial protection against same-origin XSS) as three separate guarantees.

history.title: Auth
gaps: Explained "why mobile favors tokens over cookies" as being about mobile apps being closer to hardware / avoiding the effort of replicating browser security, rather than the actual mechanism: cookies are a browser-only feature a native app never has access to in the first place.

history.title: Linked Lists
gaps: Two related misconceptions surfaced: (1) assuming a linked list's O(1) splice cost applies to 'reorder by content' operations that still require an O(n) search; (2) assuming a pointer to a node in a singly-linked list also grants access to the pointer that would need to change to delete it (its predecessor). Both stem from under-weighting the 'do I already have the pointer I need' precondition -- worth a light confirm-only check next review.

Resolved via the fixed-increment vs. doubling worked comparison taught immediately after (see taught event).

Q3: correct prediction, zero justification — surfaced as a genuine prerequisite gap, not an Arrays-specific misunderstanding. Craig has not yet been taught that a geometric series with any ratio > 1 sums to a bounded constant multiple of its largest term (the general fact that would let him prove the x1.5 case rather than guess it). Flagged for revisit — natural home is Discrete Math (sequences/series) later in the Foundations track, but worth a lighter early pass here given it is already blocking dynamic-array reasoning specifically.

history.title: Binary Search Trees (BST)
gaps: Misconception surfaced on a follow-up: concluded that a node with no left child (search for 42 terminated at node 50) must be the minimum of the *entire* tree. Corrected via a constructed counterexample (root 60, left child 20, 20 right child 50, 50 no left child) showing 20 < 50, so 50 is only the minimum of its own subtree, not the whole tree. Root-cause: conflated "no smaller value found on the path taken" with "no smaller value exists anywhere."

history.title: Binary Search Trees (BST)
gaps: BST deletion (node with two children), first attempt: proposed the parent directly adopting both children ("grandparent inherits"), which is mechanically impossible — a node only has one child-pointer slot per side, so two subtrees cannot be attached to one slot. Corrected via a concrete example (deleting 50 with children 30 and 60 under parent 70).

Second attempt: proposed always promoting the immediate right child (60) into the deleted node's spot. Works only when that right child itself has no left child; extending the scenario (giving 60 a left child, 55) exposed the collision (60 could not take both 55 and 30 as left child). Craig then correctly derived, from a hint tying back to the earlier min-finding rule, that walking left-until-empty inside the right subtree always lands on a node with at most one child (a right child, or none) — the general-purpose successor property that makes deletion always safe. Deletion itself (splicing the successor value into place) was paused before being fully executed, to be picked up next session.

BST insertion, first scenario (insert 35): walked the comparison path correctly (50 → 30 → 40) but concluded the new value "displaces" the existing node 40, making 40 a child of 35 — a genuine misconception (insertion never moves existing nodes; the walk always terminates at an empty pointer, never an occupied node). Corrected explicitly.
